blocks.title: Common-Source Amplifier
blocks.body: The Common-Source (CS) amplifier is the fundamental building block in analog MOS design, providing moderate-to-high voltage gain and high input impedance. The gate receives the input AC signal, the drain provides the amplified inverted output, and the source is tied to AC ground.

blocks.caption: Discrete NMOS common-source amplifier with four-resistor resistive divider bias

blocks.title: Small-Signal Voltage Gain
blocks.note: For $r_o \gg R_D$ with source bypassed by $C_S$, the unloaded midband gain simplifies to $A_v \approx -g_m R_D$.

blocks.title: MOS Transconductance in Saturation
blocks.tex: g_m = \sqrt{2 \mu_n C_{ox} \left(\frac{W}{L}\right) I_D} = \frac{2 I_D}{V_{GS} - V_{th}} = \mu_n C_{ox} \left(\frac{W}{L}\right) (V_{GS} - V_{th})
blocks.note: Requires operation in saturation: $V_{DS} \ge V_{GS} - V_{th}$ and $V_{GS} > V_{th}$.

blocks.title: Gain Calculation Example
blocks.body: Given $I_D = 1.0\,\mathrm{mA}$, $k_n' (W/L) = 8\,\mathrm{mA/V^2}$, $R_D = 4.7\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$, and $\lambda \approx 0$ ($r_o \to \infty$). The transconductance is $g_m = \sqrt{2 \times 8 \times 1} = 4\,\mathrm{mA/V} = 4\,\mathrm{mS}$. Therefore, the small-signal gain is $A_v = -g_m R_D = -(4\times 10^{-3})(4.7\times 10^3) = -18.8\,\mathrm{V/V}$.

blocks.title: Saturation Constraint & Clipping
blocks.body: Ensure the DC drain voltage satisfies $V_D > V_G - V_{th}$ at all times. A large output negative swing can push the transistor out of saturation into the triode region, causing severe harmonic distortion.

points: Common-Source configuration produces a $180^\circ$ phase shift between input and output.
Input gate resistance is virtually infinite at low-to-medium frequencies due to the oxide layer.
Voltage gain is proportional to transconductance $g_m$ and drain load resistance $R_D$.

questions: What happens to the small-signal gain if source resistor $R_S$ is unbypassed?
